name: Wei Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. These are pictures of the future, not predictions. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Hartmann and Sons, a family-run wholesaler of car and van parts. We supply about two hundred independent garages. I start at seven with the parts lists from the supplier reps, brake pads, filters, belts, and I know most of the part numbers by heart. I spend the day on the phone and checking the stockroom, and I like to be back by six for supper with the children.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the garages depend on me. If a mechanic in a small town can't get a gasket, the car sits there and the customer is angry, so I take it personally. What wears me out is the pressure on prices, because the big chains undercut us. My wife Anna works mornings at the church nursery, and we've got Peter, twelve, and Hanna, nine. We sing in the church choir on Thursdays, which is the one evening I switch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's nothing new. Every few years there's a system that's meant to change everything, and then we go back to doing it the way that works. I'd tell the lads at work not to be fussed, because a car part is a car part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine with it, as long as they leave me out of it. I don't use those tools and I don't plan to. If they make the reports automatic, somebody younger can press the button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I've done it for twenty years. I'd keep my notebook of part numbers and the rep names. I'd also keep paying the mortgage on time and say no to anything we don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, but not easy. It feels like carrying the same bag up the same hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never used an AI tool. What would small automations mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have hardly any savings, maybe two weeks of bills. Hartmann pays me less than the big chains would, but I stay because the old man treated me well. There are almost no other wholesalers near us, so I can't just move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the pressures on you and Anna already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the van needed new tyres and we paid for it by skipping the summer holiday. We'll skip it again if we have to. It's not a hardship, it's what you do.

say: I'd tell the lads not to be fussed, because a **car part** is a car part.
I'd say every few years a system promises to change everything.
think: I'd be fine as long as they leave me out of the tools; **younger** staff can press the button.
With two weeks of savings and almost no nearby wholesalers I can't just move.
do: Keep my **notebook** of part numbers and rep names as it is.
Keep paying the mortgage on time and say no to **extras**.
Skip the summer holiday again if money gets tight.
feel: **Settled** but not easy, like carrying the same bag up the same hill.
S0.quote: Last year the van needed new tyres and we paid for it by skipping the summer holiday.
fieldNote: Wei's anxiety comes from **money and loyalty**: low pay, no savings, no other wholesalers nearby.
He keeps his old notebook method and plans to dodge the tools.
He treats hardship as duty, not complaint.

steps.text: Keep the part-number notebook and call the reps as always
Skip the summer holiday again if the van needs money
Put twenty a week into a separate savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a machine can order a brake pad, but it can't judge a rep. At the pub or church hall I'd say it's good to have technology, but we shouldn't discard people who've given their working lives to firms. I wouldn't say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried. Ordering and price checks are most of what my junior colleagues do, and if a program does that then the family will ask why they need a senior man. I'm among the best, but that matters less if a machine is cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work harder and make myself useful in ways a computer isn't. I'd take on the garage calls, the awkward customers, and the suppliers who need talking round. I'd let one of the younger staff help me with the software, but I wouldn't be the one in front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a little insulted. I know my trade better than any screen. It feels as if the value of experience is being thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your buying job could software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners and the consultants. A family firm should look after its people, and when the founder's grandson takes over and brings in outsiders, loyalty goes. I'd say so politely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you hold responsible for how this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm moves slowly, I'm probably fine. If it moves fast, I'd be the first expensive person on the list. That's what keeps me awake.

say: I'd say a machine can order a brake pad but **can't judge a rep**.
I'd say firms shouldn't discard people who gave their working lives.
think: If a program does the ordering, the family will ask why they need a **senior man**.
If the firm moves fast, I'm the first **expensive person** on the list.
do: Take on the **garage calls**, awkward customers and suppliers who need talking round.
Let a younger colleague handle the software while I stay behind them.
Keep quiet online and speak politely at the next owners' meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit insulted that experience is being thrown out.
S1.quote: A family firm should look after its people, and when the founder's grandson takes over and brings in outsiders, loyalty goes.
fieldNote: Wei expects to be **expensive and exposed** if the firm moves fast.
He blames owners and outsiders rather than the technology.
His plan is to be useful in human work, but he does not plan to learn the tools.

steps.text: Take on the garage customer calls and tricky supplier talks
Wait to see how fast the owners move before applying anywhere
Cut the family's eating out and the kids' extra clubs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should sit down with the owners right away. At church I'd probably ask for prayers and for people to help each other. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd lose the job, and I think within two years. Buying is thinking work, and I have no skills in these systems. I'm forty-three, I've a mortgage and two children. It's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending hard and ask Anna to take more nursery hours. I'd go to my brother-in-law, who owns a garage, and ask about weekend work and whether he could use a parts man. I'd ask the church about any member who's hiring. I'd rather do honest manual work than sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, and ashamed to say so. A man is supposed to provide, and I'd feel I had failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do the first week after you hear this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children that Dad's job is changing, that we'll get through, and that we trust God and work hard. I'd keep the numbers from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that gives you a cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family and church. My parents live twenty minutes away and would take the children. The church has a fund for people in trouble, and I've paid into it for years. Robots arriving later also mean garage work lasts a few years longer.

say: I'd ask the owners to **sit down** with us right away.
At church I'd ask for prayers and for members to help each other.
think: I'd lose the job within **two years**, since buying is thinking work and I have no skills in these systems.
I'd feel I had failed as a provider.
do: Cut spending **hard** and ask Anna for more nursery hours.
Ask my brother-in-law about **weekend work** at his garage.
Ask the church about members who are hiring.
feel: **Afraid**, and ashamed to say so, because a man is supposed to provide.
S2.quote: A man is supposed to provide, and I'd feel I had failed.
fieldNote: Wei sees the job loss as **likely**, and his shame is as strong as his fear.
His cushion is family and church, not savings.
He prefers honest manual work to waiting.

steps.text: Cut spending hard and ask Anna for more nursery hours
Ask my parents and the church fund for help if needed
Do weekend parts work at my brother-in-law's garage
Tell Peter and Hanna that work is changing and we'll cope

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and I'd tell the owners to use it well. At church I'd say we should help the young ones into trades. I'd keep out of it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still think the job goes. But with five years I'd have a chance to move into something real, like running a garage's parts counter, where people still need hands and eyes. Robots take until 2034 to do hands-on work, so a trade is the better bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a training course in vehicle servicing in the evenings, and ask my brother-in-law to let me shadow him. I'd save a little more each month and keep Anna's hours at the nursery. I'd learn one computer program for stock, the plainest one, because at least then I can say I tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, with some steadiness. Five years is the difference between a shock and a hard slog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What can you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the world is changing but a good trade and an honest day's work still count. I'd bring Peter to the garage on Saturdays so he sees the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm slow with new things, I'll admit. But I've never been afraid of work, and five years lets me do it properly.

say: I'd tell the owners five years is a **fair warning** and should be used well.
At church I'd say we should help young people into **trades**.
think: I'd still think the job goes, but five years lets me move into something with hands and eyes.
Robots take until **2034** to do hands-on work, so a trade is the better bet.
do: Start an evening course in **vehicle servicing** and shadow my brother-in-law.
Learn the plainest **stock program** so I can say I tried.
Take Peter to the garage on Saturdays.
feel: **Worried**, with some steadiness; five years is the difference between a shock and a hard slog.
S3.quote: I've never been afraid of work, and five years lets me do it properly.
fieldNote: Wei turns to **hands-on trades**, matching the later robot date.
He admits he is slow with new things but trusts his work ethic.
He plans to teach his son by example.

steps.text: Start an evening course in vehicle servicing
Shadow my brother-in-law at his garage on Saturdays
Take Peter to the garage on Saturdays to see the work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and we should get on with life. At church I'd say the children need good schooling and a trade. Online I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd carry on as I am for a while, and that's the honest truth. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, with the mortgage almost done. I'd look at moving into garage work around year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the mortgage down, put some aside for each child, and take that servicing course in a few years. I'd also tell the owners I'm happy to train the next buyer, so I have a place if they keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though never fully. A decade lets me breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. What do you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'll have it harder, because everything will be quicker. I'd tell my children to get a skill with their hands as well as their heads, and to stay close to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different for your children's generation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry a bit less for myself than for them. I'd still want a plan, but I'd have time to build it slowly.

At church I'd say children need good schooling and a **trade**.
think: I'd carry on as I am for a while, with the **mortgage** nearly done by 2036.
I worry less for myself than for my children.
do: Pay the **mortgage** down and put some aside for each child.
Take the servicing course in a few years.
Offer to train the **next buyer** so I keep a place.
feel: **Calmer**, though never fully; a decade lets me breathe.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to get a skill with their hands as well as their heads, and to stay close to family.
fieldNote: Ten years brings **calm**, though his thin cushion keeps him anxious.
He worries more for his children than for himself.

steps.text: Pay the mortgage down faster and save for each child
Take the vehicle servicing course within three years
Teach Peter and Hanna a hands-on skill
Offer to train the next buyer at Hartmann and Sons

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I've got almost no savings and no skills in the new systems, and there's hardly another wholesaler nearby. What would help is fair warning from the owners, a chance to learn a trade properly with pay, and the church and family around us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: That people like me aren't against change. We're against being dropped after twenty years of loyalty. Give an honest man a chance to learn and he'll work harder than anyone.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against change. We're against being dropped after twenty years of loyalty. Give an honest man a chance to learn and he'll work harder than anyone.
portrait: Wei Kowalski, 43, is senior **buyer** at a family car-parts wholesaler, with a nursery-worker wife, two kids and a mortgage.
He's traditional, churchgoing and **resistant**: he uses a notebook of part numbers and never uses AI tools.
Thin savings, low pay and almost no nearby wholesalers leave him anxious even when little changes.
He expects buying to go and turns to **family**, church and hands-on trades.
He blames owners and outsiders for dropping loyal staff, not the technology itself.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, with almost no savings and no skills in the new systems.
whatWouldHelp: Fair **warning** from owners, paid training in a trade and the support of family and church.
